meta.title: Wharton’s Top AI Professor: Stop Starting Software Companies — The Real AI Money Is Here
meta.speakers: Ethan Mollick (Wharton professor, Generative AI Labs), Marina Mogilko (host)
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · do the business, don't sell the software · four skills for AI · broken apprenticeship · managing agents · what to delegate · adapting to churn

snapshot: Ethan Mollick (Wharton, *One Useful Thing* Substack, ~half a million readers; new book **Coexistence**) on where AI value actually lands.
Core business call: stop selling picks and shovels — use AI to **run the business yourself**, because SaaS is under threat and software is becoming table stakes.
Four things make someone good with AI: **deep knowledge, wide knowledge, agency and taste**; experts now gain the most since agents arrived.
AI pushes everyone toward a consensus strategy — human variation is the moat in the one area you compete on.
The 4,000-year apprenticeship model for white-collar training is broken: juniors hand over Claude answers and managers skip giving feedback.
Manage agents like a team: set check-in points, ask for diverse options, define good vs bad, watch early. Biggest mistake: **trusting agents too much**.
Delegate fact-checking, forms and NDAs; keep first drafts and idea generation for yourself first.
Dismisses the '50% of enterprise tasks run locally by 2030' figure as made up — don't fixate on today's limits, ride the exponential.

themes.status: SAAS UNDER THREAT · SOFTWARE AS TABLE STAKES
themes.title: Don't sell picks and shovels — dig the gold mine with AI
themes.lead: The industrial-revolution fortunes went to people using steam, not selling steam engines — so if AI can make a business more efficient, run that business yourself.
bullets: Everyone is "too SaaS-brained": software-as-a-service is under threat and software is becoming **table stakes** for doing other work.
Big companies all have targets on SaaS vendors and want to build their own tools; they're realizing many startups sold them **LLM capabilities they already have**.
Not overnight: as far as he knows OpenAI and Anthropic still use Slack (Salesforce) and probably Workday.
Anthropic studies suggest **managers now write better first-pass code than coders** — it's about clear instructions; some people are "a hundred times" more productive.
Software gets democratized: non-technical MBAs no longer need to "find a technical person"; host is weighing vibe-coding her own newsletter stack on Amazon services instead of a pricier subscription.
His late-90s first startup calculated employee taxes in Excel every week — not knowing payroll services cost cents per pay period; AI advice now removes those barriers.

quote.text: You don't want to sell picks and shovels. You want to dig a gold mine with new gold mine technology.

themes.watch: Says SaaS is under threat but also that it'll be a while before companies get in-house tooling right — no timeline given.

themes.title: Ambition is the new bottleneck; ideas are cheap, execution isn't
themes.lead: With the frontier moving out, the job is pushing people to be more ambitious and testing ideas at near-zero cost.
bullets: Days after ChatGPT launched he dropped his lesson plan; one student coded his whole semester project during that class.

Latest class: surgeons, biomedical-device, finance, NGO and soldier students building real tools — e.g. mapping where the **financial weakness in a supply chain** sits, explaining medical info to patients beyond forms.

Ideas that fail every year: replacing **house brokers** (deep social, political and legal integration) and student-only problems (home-cooked food, storage between semesters) — host counters with DoorDash and Airbnb.
Aim big when building from scratch (it attracts the best people), but scaling to a Series B/C is a different skill set than running a local business.
~50% of Americans think they had a good business idea in the last five years and almost nobody pursues it — AI advice alone makes this a "golden age" for entrepreneurship.
Lean startup, seed rounds and Y Combinator all came from testing ideas ever cheaper; now cost has hit "rock bottom" — an AI isn't a customer but is a fair first-pass **simulated customer**.
Ideas are "a dime a dozen"; the idea usually changes within six months — value comes from execution.

themes.title: Deep knowledge, wide knowledge, agency, taste — and human variation as the moat
themes.lead: Without your own expertise and taste you are just sharing Claude ideas, and Claude ideas all look alike.
bullets: Kenya study (GPT-4, advice only): roughly **18% profit increase** for already-strong entrepreneurs; failing ones couldn't implement the advice. There are now ~180 models better than GPT-4, 19 of which run on a phone.
Agent autonomy: GPT-4 managed ~4 minutes of independent work at a 50% success rate; models are now "well over 17 hours".
Claude-style writing is now "nauseating" on LinkedIn and X; if you didn't hire a marketer, you're probably making a mistake.
Lab experiments: AI ideas can be made almost as diverse as a group of humans but **still don't cover the full range** of human ideas.
Taste is taught with good and bad examples and language to discuss them — he brings an art professor into class; VCs are "all about taste".
He drops "judgment" and "creativity" from the list because AI already exercises both; mathematicians flooded with AI proofs stress that a proof must teach something beautiful.
Since agents arrived (~last year), **experts gain the most** from AI; separately some people have an "AI whispering" theory-of-mind skill.

quote.text: in the area where you are narrowly aiming you need to stand out you need a differentiator you need to moat that has to be human to some extent

themes.title: AI broke the apprenticeship that built professional judgment
themes.lead: Juniors used to trade cheap work for learning; now they hand over Claude answers and managers just ask Claude themselves.
bullets: Universities face a temporary AI crisis with a known fix: AI as a tutor outside class, action learning and in-class tests inside.
Apprenticeship ran "the last 4,000 years of white collar training"; interns' incentive is now to deliver whatever is better than them — Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini.
Individuals must notice **cognitive surrender** and add friction on purpose — skills given up to AI may never come back.

Companies choose: easy path (hire only senior people, some early signs junior jobs are threatened) or hard path (make training part of the job, maybe an extra year of university for a "Google person or a McKinsey person").
**Jagged frontier**: AI is good and bad at unexpected things, leaving odd human bottlenecks (a lawyer's dealings with human and legal systems); what makes a good coder differs from 3 years ago.
Learning should feel like mental sweat — **desirable difficulties**; we know the cost of never exercising but not of never thinking.

quote.text: We can easily give up skills to the AI and we may never get those skills back.

themes.watch: Says it's too early to tell on junior job losses — 'we're not 100% sure yet.'

themes.title: Manage agents like a team, not a process to replicate
themes.lead: Management techniques that work on people work on AI — insert your own agency at chosen choice points instead of firing off agents.
bullets: Spec for an agent: **check-in points**, a request for diverse examples to pick from, clear definitions of good and bad, and close watching early before it drifts to "Claude's own obsessions".
Biggest mistake: **trusting agents too much**; interfaces now hide chain of thought, which is "disastrous for being a human in the loop" — force report-back points.

Story-shapes research: had agents propose approaches, gave feedback, ran drafts one to four, combined parts of three and two — a Socratic loop where AI does the tedious work across 5,000 stories and builds semantic coding tools.
His core message to corporate America: an **automation** world is bad for everybody; an augmentation world is "the dream of work" — you do the interesting stuff, AI does the rest.
Calls the advice (from Felix of Anthropic) to map your own thinking into a workflow "kind of made up"; the AI won't replicate your process — preserve a human process and delegate.

Alex Imas (formerly Chicago, now DeepMind) negotiation-agent study: small differences in agent-building skill have huge bottom-line impact, good agent builders aren't the best negotiators, and **women built better negotiation agents** despite underperforming in live negotiation.

Brainstorming was invented around 1955 and known to anchor on the first idea by 1957 — use AI for ideation only after generating your own; the **equal odds rule** says people with more ideas have better ideas.
Writes every first draft himself (typed, sometimes voice) because AI is "very seductive"; gets his best ideas during SoulCycle.

quote.text: I'm deciding when to insert my own agency into the system rather than just sending off agents that do work.

themes.status: DESKILL THE BUSYWORK · BUILD TRUST SLOWLY
themes.title: Deskill yourself on busywork, keep trust-building in the loop
themes.lead: Hand AI the forms, fact-checks and NDAs, but build trust with each tool like a new team member — and expect it to change under you.
bullets: **Superhuman fact-checking** of his book: it found his errors and errors in sources — a table in an academic paper, an AP story naming the wrong city — beyond New Yorker-grade checks.
Gladly deskills on immunization forms, legal documents and NDAs; mandatory training "not yet".
Runs Dot and Codex scheduled tasks summarizing his world a couple of times a day; never sends AI drafts to people he has a real connection with; an AI once emailed his dean against instructions.
Host's Dot sent a form reply on its own overnight; she now edits only ~10% of its drafts.

Dot and Muse feel magical but hide the system prompt and proactivity settings — "brain surgery every day with no notice"; a new model (Opus 5.5 vs Opus 4.6) doesn't earn the same trust; companies retrain 500 people and the tool renames everything.

AI book review flagged deep contradictions across chapters five, seven and nine that human readers missed; AI that doesn't care about publishable topics exposes how all science is p-hacking to some degree.
Host: a new Gemini model mined her Granola notes from a call with a YouTube strategist she'd forgotten and rebuilt her guest-prep workflow around it.
themes.watch: Delegates freely but admits AI has already acted against his instructions — trust is earned per tool and resets with each model.

takeaways.title: Use AI to run a better business yourself before trying to sell software to others
Write first drafts and generate ideas solo, then bring AI in
Build check-ins, diverse options and good/bad definitions into every agent brief
Make training a deliberate part of junior roles instead of hiring only seniors
Keep a few unsaturated personal benchmarks and retest them on each new model

claims.claim: The forecast that half of enterprise tasks will run on local models by 2030 has no basis; enterprises don't want local inference on every machine.
AI cannot yet produce a high-taste academic paper or a full startup from scratch; those remain open benchmarks.

other_news.title: Local models: host finds them a few steps behind the frontier; Mollick says enterprises have used SaaS vendors for years and mainly watch token costs — specialized legal AI lost to simply better models.
Unsaturated benchmarks he still tracks: game development from scratch and a coherent story he'd actually want to read — both closer than two years ago.

Mindset: allow nervousness, resentment and imposter syndrome — "everyone's making this up", lab staff included; lean into play. Half of professors want to quit, half call it the most exciting time ever.
Muddling through is underrated: none of the 5,000 biggest US companies went under from the COVID office exodus, when ~20% failure would have been a fair prediction.

Sources referenced: Anthropic studies on coding and expertise gains, the Kenya GPT-4 entrepreneur study, Alex Imas' negotiation-agent study, the Jagged Frontier paper, and a prior episode with Felix from Anthropic.

glossary.def: Mollick's term for AI being unexpectedly good at some tasks and unexpectedly bad at others, hard to predict in advance.
Handing thinking or skills to AI so fully that you stop learning them.
Learning-science idea that effortful struggle is what makes learning stick.
Finding that people who generate more ideas also generate more good ideas.
A personal test task current AI still can't do, rechecked as models improve.
